title: Life Cycles & Development Approaches

header.html: Process Task 1 Develop an integrated project management plan and plan delivery — assess project needs, complexity and magnitude; recommend a project management development approach (predictive, adaptive/agile or hybrid); recommend a project execution strategy. Also the exam-wide split: about 40% predictive, 60% adaptive/agile and hybrid, across all three domains.

Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

html:
1Core Definitions

Term Meaning
Project life cycle The series of phases a project passes through; independent of the product life cycle (which the project may only be part of)
Project phase A collection of logically related activities that culminates in one or more deliverables and/or outcomes; phases may be sequential, transitional or overlapping
Phase gate A review (also stage gate, gate review, iteration review, decision point review) held to confirm exit criteria were met before the next phase
Development approach The means used to create and evolve the product, service or result during the life cycle: predictive, adaptive or hybrid. Not the same as the "development phase" (the stage where deliverables are built and tested)
Integrated baseline The scope, schedule and cost baselines taken together (predictive)
Timebox / iteration A fixed period (often 1 to 4 weeks in agile methods) in which a chosen set of work is completed and demonstrated
Iterative Refines and improves the project through repeated cycles
Incremental Delivers the final product in small, usable segments, each providing value and building on the last
Delivery cadence How often outcomes are delivered: single, multiple, periodic or continuous
Focus Areas Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring and Controlling, Closing (formerly Process Groups); not phases

2Project Phases and Phase Gates

  • Phase attributes can include name, number, duration, resource requirements, entrance criteria and exit criteria.
  • Exit criteria may tie to acceptance criteria, contractual obligations or performance targets; entry criteria may involve resource availability, verified viability and alignment with organizational goals.
  • A gate compares performance and progress with project and business documents and leads to a decision: continue to the next phase; continue with modification; end the project or phase; remain in the phase; repeat the phase or parts of it; or park the project temporarily (e.g., for an urgent initiative). Often described as a go/no-go decision.
  • Gates normally sit at the end of a phase, but can also sit at the start (pre-phase gates) to check alignment, resources, planning and risks before proceeding.
  • Organizations often standardize a few life cycles; if none is prescribed, the team picks the best one. A life cycle should be flexible: choose the development approach (or mix), the processes and activities, and adjust phase attributes.

Typical variables over time (predictive example):

  • Cost and staffing: low at the start, rise during the work, drop rapidly at the end.
  • Risk and uncertainty: greatest at the start; fall as decisions are made and deliverables accepted.
  • Stakeholder influence on change: highest at the start (can raise value without large cost or schedule impact); falls as the project progresses; the cost of changes rises. In adaptive work, stakeholders participate actively in execution, so risks are detected earlier through consistent feedback.

3The Three Development Approaches

  • Approaches are a spectrum: predictive at one end, adaptive at the other, hybrid a mix.
  • The project manager, in consultation with the project management team, usually chooses the approach based on the requirements, scope, timeline and goals; organization culture and needs; stakeholder involvement; risk profile; technology; and overall complexity.
  • Requirements clear and stable early → predictive may be best; schedule and cost baselines are set from the scope to be delivered.
  • Requirements unclear, or high complexity and uncertainty → more feedback needed → adaptive: work is reviewed in timeboxes so feedback can be incorporated as the integrated baseline evolves; at the end of each timebox, implemented requirements are reviewed and the next timebox planned.

3.1 Fixed and variable constraints (the inverted triangle)

  • Scope fixed: unexpected changes are absorbed by altering budget or schedule.
  • Budget and schedule fixed: unexpected changes are absorbed by varying scope (typical for timeboxed agile work).

4Predictive Approaches

Also called waterfall, plan-driven or traditional.

  • Best when scope can be stabilized early; large investment or regulatory oversight; scope, schedule, cost, resources, quality requirements and risks can be well defined early and stay relatively stable. Allows much of the planning to be done up front.
  • Requires robust change control and planned re-evaluation between phases.
  • Especially suited when the cost of iterating far exceeds its value (the build phase of many construction projects) and in heavily regulated environments such as healthcare, where regulators require phase gates.
  • Incremental delivery inside a predictive project: overall scope is well understood and planned up front, but delivery is phased because of size, complexity or risk. Each increment builds on the previous one; stakeholders can use parts of the product early while scope and timeline remain largely fixed and change stays controlled.
  • Typical life cycle: feasibility → design → build → check → transfer → close.

5Adaptive Approaches

Also called change-driven or agile.

  • Best when requirements and the technical solution are highly uncertain and volatile and likely to change significantly. A clear vision is set at the start; initial requirements are progressively elaborated, changed or replaced with stakeholder feedback, the environment or unexpected events.
  • Can be iterative and incremental. Some agile methods use iterations of 1 to 4 weeks with a demonstration at the end; the whole team helps plan: it selects achievable scope from the prioritized product backlog, estimates the work and builds collaboratively.
  • Flow-based scheduling: optimizes the flow of work through the system, maximizes throughput and minimizes waste. Drawn from the Kanban method (visual workflow management that limits work in process (WIP) based on lean principles, with continuous delivery without overburdening the team) and the theory of constraints (find and address the most significant limiting factor).
  • Agile is a mindset broader than any framework; agile approaches are considered adaptive. Methods differ in breadth (how much of the life cycle they cover) and depth (how prescriptive); examples: Scrum, XP, Kanban, Lean, FDD, DSDM, Crystal, Agile UP, SAFe, LeSS, Scrum of Scrums. A method is a systematic series of steps; a tool kit (e.g., PMI Disciplined Agile) is a collection of tools and techniques to choose from.
  • Well suited to: design projects, new product development (features refined by market needs), digital/software projects with evolving scope, uncertainty and a need for early or incremental delivery.

6Hybrid Approaches

A combination of adaptive and predictive elements. PMBOK 8 notes that most modern projects benefit from a hybrid approach: flexibility to adapt while keeping control over predictable aspects.

Why hybrid Examples
Uncertainty or risk around requirements early, then a stable build Custom home: iterate on the design, build once
Deliverables can be modularized or built by different teams One deliverable adaptive (software), another predictive (data center build)
Different phases suit different approaches; one approach dominates with subsidiary streams in another Smart-building construction (predictive) with flexible IT systems (adaptive); hospital records system with predictive infrastructure and adaptive user-interface work

PMI Disciplined Agile hybrid levels: Level 1 predictive dominates, some adaptive elements reduce pain points; Level 2 both contribute significantly; Level 3 adaptive dominates, some predictive elements satisfy business constraints.

7Choosing the Approach: Selection Factors

Category Factor Pushes toward
Deliverables Degree of innovation (new or complex technology or business model) Adaptive
Requirements certainty (well known, easy to define) Predictive
Scope stability (less stable) Adaptive
Ease of change (change difficult or costly) Predictive
Delivery options (deliverable can be delivered in components or progressively elaborated) Adaptive/hybrid
Risk (to manage uncertainty) Adaptive
Safety requirements (rigorous; much up-front planning) Predictive
Feedback (significant value from frequent end-user feedback) Adaptive
Regulations (heavy oversight: processes, documentation, demonstration) Predictive
Project Stakeholders (adaptive calls for significant involvement) Adaptive
Schedule constraints (value in early partial delivery vs fixed end date) Adaptive vs Predictive
Financing uncertainty Adaptive/iterative
Size and complexity (larger, complex, evolving) Flexible approaches
Team experience and skills (communication, collaboration, problem-solving) Adaptive
Interdependencies on other projects, departments, functions Iterative
Organization Structure (fixed functional and hierarchical vs network-oriented) Predictive vs adaptive/hybrid
Culture (managing and directing vs embraces uncertainty, self-managed teams, innovation) Predictive vs adaptive
Capability (policies, ways of working, reporting, attitudes aligned; maturity of processes) Whichever the organization can support
Team size and location (adaptive often works with 3 to 9 members; some methods favor colocation; remote can also be efficient) Adaptive (small teams)

Different deliverables in the same project may use different approaches.

8Delivery Cadence

Cadence Meaning Example
Single delivery All outcomes delivered at the end Process re-engineering rolled out at the end
Multiple deliveries Components delivered at different times (sequentially or in parallel) Drug development stages; building security upgrades (barriers, badges, keypads)
Periodic deliveries Multiple deliveries on a regular, fixed schedule (common in adaptive) Internal releases every 2 weeks, periodic market releases
Continuous delivery Incrementally delivering value to production on an ongoing basis; product always production-ready; automation; frequent, low-risk deployment Teams deploying tested increments continuously

In all cases deliveries must be concluded so as to meet or exceed target business objectives.

9The Five Project Management Focus Areas

Focus Areas are the fundamental actions of any project regardless of approach. They are implemented through formal processes, informal practices or policies; they may be iterative, continuous and overlapping, and are not project phases (some phase names may coincide). They are independent of industry and application area.

Focus Area Purpose and content Key benefit
Initiating Define a new project or phase; usually formal authorization. Align stakeholder expectations with the project's purpose; define initial scope; commit initial funds; identify stakeholders; assign PM roles. Artifacts: project charter, stakeholder register; business documents (business case, benefits management plan) originate outside the project and are inputs; the sponsor gives the minimum information needed to start Projects are authorized only when aligned with strategic objectives and with business case, benefits and stakeholders considered from the start; shared understanding of success criteria
Planning Establish the intended scope, define and refine objectives, develop the course of action. Artifacts: product backlog, project management plan. Planning is progressive, iterative or rolling wave; progressive elaboration = ongoing refinement of the plan. Predictive front-loads planning; iterative does brief high-level planning ("roadmapping") then frequent replanning Defines the course of action to complete the project or phase
Executing Complete the work consistent with the currently agreed course of action: coordinate resources, manage stakeholder engagement, perform activities. The plan can and should change whenever the change enhances value. The choice of approach shows most here Focused execution to achieve the value proposition in the integrated baseline
Monitoring & Controlling Monitoring: compare actual with planned performance, produce measures, report. Controlling: analyze variances, assess trends, evaluate alternatives, recommend corrective actions; corrective actions are negotiated and agreed with stakeholders. Runs in parallel with the other areas; effort is steady in stable plans, irregular in adaptive work The project stays on track to meet expectations
Closing Formally complete or close a project, phase or contract, or terminate early. Verify that the other Focus Areas' actions are complete; verify outputs, outcomes and benefits; transition to operations. May address suspension or early closure when canceling is the best way to minimize negative return Phases, projects and contracts are closed properly and transitioned to operations

  • In a predictive phase, effort shifts across the Focus Areas in waves (planning heavy early, executing in the middle, closing at the end). In an adaptive project, each iteration contains planning, executing and monitoring and controlling, and the Focus Areas are revisited continually.
  • PMBOK 8 has 40 processes grouped under seven performance domains (counts: Governance 9, Scope 6, Schedule 3, Finance 4, Stakeholders 7, Resources 5, Risk 6). They are illustrative, not a prescriptive methodology.

10Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid at a Glance

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Requirements Defined up front; changes through formal change control Emerge and evolve; backlog reprioritized Fixed for stable parts, evolving for the rest
Planning Detailed up front, then updated High-level vision and roadmap, then frequent planning each iteration Detailed for predictive streams, light for adaptive ones
Delivery Single or phased/incremental; value mostly late Frequent increments, early value Mixed cadence
Scope / time / cost Scope fixed; time and cost estimated and baselined Time and cost fixed per iteration; scope varies Mixed
Customer involvement Milestones, reviews, acceptance Continuous Both
Change cost High late in the project Designed to be low Mixed
Governance Phase gates, comprehensive controls Lightweight; reviews each iteration Moderate/combined
Best fit Stable requirements, regulation, safety, fixed date, costly iteration Uncertain, innovative, volatile, early feedback valuable Mixed deliverables; most real projects
Team Any size; hierarchical culture Small teams (often 3 to 9), self-managing culture Depends

11Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. Match the approach to the context, not to preference. Stable and regulated → predictive; uncertain and feedback-rich → adaptive; mixed → hybrid. About 60% of exam items involve agile or hybrid situations, so be comfortable in both worlds.
  2. Hybrid is a legitimate, often best answer when the scenario mixes fixed and uncertain elements (e.g., hardware plus software).
  3. Incremental ≠ iterative. Increments deliver usable parts; iterations refine through cycles. Agile usually does both.
  4. Focus Areas are not phases. Do not answer "planning is finished" literally; planning, monitoring and replanning continue (progressive elaboration, rolling wave).
  5. The plan may change when change adds value. Executing does not mean rigidly following the baseline; use the change process.
  6. Phase gates are decision points, not rubber stamps. If exit criteria are not met or value has changed, the options include continue with modification, repeat, hold or end.
  7. Cost of change rises over time in predictive work. A late major scope request means impact analysis and change control; in adaptive work it is handled through backlog reprioritization.
  8. In fixed-budget, fixed-date agile work, scope flexes. Do not promise all scope; reprioritize.
  9. Organization culture and structure matter. A hierarchical functional organization adopting agile needs alignment of policies and reporting; consider a hybrid or incremental adoption.
  10. Closing includes verifying outputs, outcomes and benefits, not just handing over deliverables.

12Exam Q&A

12.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1A hospital must implement a regulated medical-device system with stable requirements, mandatory phase reviews and strict documentation duties. Which development approach is most suitable?

  • APredictive, with phase gates and a formal change control process
  • BHybrid, with mostly adaptive delivery and documentation written afterward
  • CKanban, with continuous flow and planning limited to the board
  • DAdaptive, with two-week iterations and demonstrations for clinicians
Show the answer

Answer: A. Stable requirements, heavy regulation and mandated phase reviews favor a predictive approach with gates and formal change control. Adaptive or flow-based delivery would not produce the documentation and approvals the regulator expects.

S2A start-up is building a new mobile app. Requirements are unclear, competitors move quickly, and early user feedback is expected to reshape the features. What should the project manager recommend?

  • AA predictive approach that locks the scope before development starts
  • BA phased plan with formal sign-offs at the end of each long stage
  • CAn adaptive approach with short iterations and regular demonstrations
  • DA single delivery at the end so that rework is kept to a minimum
Show the answer

Answer: C. High uncertainty and valuable early feedback point to an adaptive approach, where short iterations let the team learn and reprioritize. Locking scope or delaying delivery removes the feedback that should drive the product.

S3A bank's mandatory release process, with fixed change windows and audit sign-offs, will govern a payments upgrade, but the team wants short feedback loops to cut rework. Which hybrid description fits?

  • APredictive dominates, with some adaptive elements added to reduce pain points
  • BAdaptive dominates, with predictive elements kept only to satisfy the audit rules
  • CBoth approaches contribute equally, so the team picks one for each task every day
  • DFully predictive, because adaptive practices cannot coexist with change windows
Show the answer

Answer: A. With a mandatory gated process in charge and feedback loops added to cut rework, predictive dominates and adaptive elements ease the pain points, which is the first of the hybrid levels. The other options describe an adaptive-led or balanced mix, or deny that mixing is possible.

S4A phase review finds that two of the five exit criteria are unmet, yet the contractors for the next phase are already mobilizing. What should the project manager do?

  • ARecord the criteria as met to avoid the contractors' standby costs
  • BReport the unmet criteria and let the gate authority choose to modify or repeat
  • CStart the next phase and finish the open criteria in parallel
  • DCancel the project because the gate was not passed at the first attempt
Show the answer

Answer: B. A gate is a decision point: with unmet criteria the options include continuing with modification, repeating the phase or parts of it, remaining in the phase or ending it, and the authority decides on the facts. Pushing ahead, misreporting or canceling outright skips that decision.

S5A team releases a usable payment module in month 2, adds reporting in month 4 and analytics in month 6, each release building on the last. The full scope was defined at the start. Which delivery style is this?

  • AContinuous delivery with automated releases to production
  • BIncremental delivery within a predictive life cycle
  • CIterative delivery with the scope changing after each cycle
  • DRolling wave planning applied to the later releases only
Show the answer

Answer: B. The scope was planned in full and delivered in usable, cumulative pieces, which is incremental delivery. Iterative work refines a product through repeated cycles, and continuous delivery means production-ready releases all the time.

S6An agile team has a fixed budget and a fixed end date, and new high-priority requests keep arriving. How should the project manager handle this?

  • AAsk the sponsor to extend the budget and end date so that everything fits
  • BReject every new request in order to protect the committed scope
  • CAsk the team to work overtime until all requests are delivered
  • DReprioritize the backlog so the highest-value items fit the fixed limits
Show the answer

Answer: D. When budget and schedule are fixed, scope is the variable, so the product owner reorders the backlog by value and the lowest-value items drop out. Extending the limits, overtime or blanket refusal ignores the constraint or the value.

S7During execution, the team learns new information that requires replanning part of the schedule. A stakeholder complains that planning should have been finished at the start. What is the best response?

  • AExplain that planning is progressive and process the change appropriately
  • BFreeze the plan to protect the baseline until execution is complete
  • CRestart the project so that planning can be completed properly
  • DAgree with the stakeholder and carry on with the original schedule unchanged
Show the answer

Answer: A. Planning is progressive: the Focus Areas overlap and the plan is refined as information emerges, with changes processed through the proper route. Ignoring the information, restarting or freezing the plan would all damage value.

S8Users want to receive working features every two weeks and to give feedback each time. Which delivery cadence fits best?

  • APhase-gated delivery, with feedback only at gate reviews
  • BSingle delivery of all outcomes at the end of the project
  • CPeriodic delivery on a fixed two-week schedule
  • DMultiple deliveries, each tied to the end of a project phase
Show the answer

Answer: C. Regular fixed-interval deliveries, such as every two weeks, are periodic delivery and give users working features and a feedback point each cycle. Single, phase-bound or gate-bound delivery postpones feedback.

S9A functional, hierarchical organization asks one team to try agile. Which consideration matters most for the team's success?

  • AAdopting agile vocabulary quickly so that every team member sounds consistent
  • BGrowing the team to 25 members so that more work runs in parallel
  • CRemoving all documentation so that the team can move faster
  • DAligning policies, reporting and attitudes with the new way of working
Show the answer

Answer: D. Organizational capability, culture and structure influence whether an approach works, so policies, reporting and attitudes must be aligned or tailored, possibly toward a hybrid. Vocabulary, headcount or dropping documentation do not address those barriers.

S10Late in a predictive project, a stakeholder asks for a major scope addition. Which statement reflects the situation correctly?

  • AThe change will cost about the same as it would have at the start
  • BStakeholders can no longer request changes after the plan is approved
  • CThe project should switch to an agile approach for this request
  • DChange is typically costly late in the life cycle, so assess impact first
Show the answer

Answer: D. The cost of change rises as a predictive project progresses, so the request needs impact assessment and change control. Pretending the cost is unchanged, refusing requests or switching approach midstream does not address that.

12.2 Recall Q&As

R1What decisions can a phase gate lead to?

Show the answer

Continue, continue with modification, end the project or phase, remain in the phase, repeat the phase or elements of it, or park the project temporarily.

R2Define iterative and incremental.

Show the answer

Iterative refines through repeated cycles; incremental delivers the product in small, usable segments that build on each other.

R3Name the three development approaches and where each is optimal.

Show the answer

Predictive (stable, clear requirements; regulation; costly change), adaptive (uncertain, volatile, feedback-driven), hybrid (a mix).

R4What are the four hybrid patterns and the three DA levels?

Show the answer

Adaptive then predictive rollout; both simultaneously; mainly predictive with a small adaptive element; mainly adaptive with a predictive component. Levels: 1 predictive dominant, 2 balanced, 3 adaptive dominant.

R5What is the inverted triangle concept?

Show the answer

Choosing which constraints are fixed (scope, or budget and schedule) so the others vary to absorb change.

R6Name the four delivery cadences.

Show the answer

Single, multiple, periodic, continuous.

R7Name the five Focus Areas and say whether they are phases.

Show the answer

Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring and Controlling, Closing. They are not phases; they overlap and repeat.

R8Where are risk and uncertainty highest?

Show the answer

At the start of the project or phase; they decrease as decisions are made and deliverables accepted.

R9What is flow-based scheduling and where does it come from?

Show the answer

Optimizing the flow of work and throughput while minimizing waste; from Kanban (WIP limits) and the theory of constraints.

R10What is the typical iteration length and team size in agile methods?

Show the answer

Iterations of 1 to 4 weeks; teams of about 3 to 9 members.

R11What is the integrated baseline?

Show the answer

The scope, schedule and cost baselines together.

R12How many processes does PMBOK 8 have and how are they grouped?

Show the answer

40 processes across seven performance domains, mapped to the five Focus Areas.

13Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Approaches Predictive (plan-driven), adaptive (agile, change-driven), hybrid (mix); a spectrum
Predictive fits Stable requirements, regulation, safety, fixed date, costly iteration
Adaptive fits Uncertain, volatile, innovative, valuable early feedback, unstable scope
Hybrid Mixed deliverables; four patterns; DA levels 1 to 3; most modern projects
Iterative vs incremental Refine by cycles vs deliver usable pieces; agile does both
Iteration Timebox, often 1 to 4 weeks, demo at the end; team of about 3 to 9
Inverted triangle Scope fixed → budget/schedule vary; budget and schedule fixed → scope varies
Phase gate Compares progress with business documents; go/no-go among six outcomes; pre-phase gates possible
Over time Risk/uncertainty and stakeholder influence fall; cost of change and staffing profile rise then drop
Delivery cadence Single, multiple, periodic, continuous
Focus Areas Initiating, Planning, Executing, M&C, Closing; not phases; overlap
Planning styles Progressive elaboration, rolling wave, roadmapping + frequent replanning
Flow Kanban (WIP limits), theory of constraints
40 processes Governance 9, Scope 6, Schedule 3, Finance 4, Stakeholders 7, Resources 5, Risk 6
First-action pattern Assess needs, complexity and context; recommend the approach that fits; revisit it as conditions change
